title: Elie Wiesel survived Auschwitz, broke ten years of silence with "Night" and won the Nobel Peace Prize

trailer.text: Elie Wiesel was a Romanian-born Jewish writer, and his works are a testament to the destruction of European Jewry during World War II.
In 1944 the Holocaust reached his town, Sighet. The town's Jews were deported to Auschwitz, and there his mother and younger sister were murdered.
After the war he vowed to be silent for ten years, and only in 1956 did he publish his first book.
From this book grew "Night", which according to Israel Hayom has sold more than ten million copies.
In 1986 Wiesel won the Nobel Peace Prize, and in his speech he said that action is the only remedy to indifference.

glance.label: Best-known book
glance.value: "Night", more than ten million copies according to Israel Hayom

paragraphs.text: Elie Wiesel was born on September 30, 1928, in Sighet, Romania.
His early childhood was spent in a small Hasidic community, in a rather closed life of prayer and contemplation.

Hungary was an ally of Nazi Germany. As early as July–August 1941 hundreds of Sighet's Jews were deported from Hungary, and many of them were murdered at Kamenets-Podolsk, but most of the town's Jews were struck only after the German invasion in March 1944.
By April 1944 the Jews had been put into a ghetto, and on May 15 the deportations to Auschwitz began.
On arrival at Auschwitz, Wiesel's mother and younger sister were murdered in a gas chamber.
According to The History Place website, Dr. Josef Mengele selected Wiesel and his father for forced labor, and the two ended up at the rubber factory at Buna.
Wiesel was marked with the number A-7713.
According to the same website, young Wiesel received 25 lashes for a minor infraction.
He and his father were forced to work for eight months, and were then transferred to other concentration camps, near the end of the war.
In his Nobel lecture Wiesel described the prisoners as left without possessions and without human ties, in a social and cultural void.
He recounted there that night after night endless processions vanished into flames that lit up the sky.
According to the Nobel Prize website, in early 1945 Wiesel and his father were forced on a death march to Buchenwald, and there the father became infected with dysentery.
According to the Nobel Prize website and Britannica, the father died in Buchenwald at the end of January.
Wiesel, sixteen years old, was still alive when Allied soldiers liberated the camp on April 11.
He was freed in 1945.
According to the Holocaust Encyclopedia of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, Wiesel and his father were transferred from Auschwitz to Buchenwald, and there the father died.

stations.title: Ten years of silence, and then "Night"

paragraphs.text: After liberation Wiesel spent a few years in a French orphanage, then moved to Paris and studied literature and philosophy at the Sorbonne.
In his Nobel lecture he described a young man in Paris whose mother, father and little sister are gone, and who is alone and on the verge of despair.
He said there that after the war the people around them refused to listen, and those who listened refused to believe.
Wiesel vowed to be silent for ten years about what he had experienced in the Holocaust.
The French writer Francois Mauriac encouraged him to break the silence and tell his story.
According to Israel Hayom, Mauriac, a Nobel laureate in literature, urged him to rewrite a shortened version of the book in French.
His first book came out in 1956 in Yiddish, "And the World Remained Silent", and was a lengthy account of his life in Auschwitz.
According to AP, "Night" began as an 800-page story in Yiddish and was cut to under 300 pages for an edition in Argentina.
According to AP, the book was cut again for the French market, and in the United States it came out in 1960 at just over 100 pages.
Wiesel said in a 2002 interview that the first English printing was 3,000 copies.
According to Israel Hayom, his literary agent Georges Borchardt said that at the time no one wanted to talk about the Holocaust.
According to the same newspaper, the Eichmann trial in 1961 brought the Holocaust into mainstream discourse in the United States.
"Night" is based directly on Wiesel's experiences but is structured like a novel, and so there is an ongoing debate over how to categorize it.
The critic Ruth Franklin wrote that it is the most devastating account of the Holocaust she had read.
According to AP, in 2006 a new translation returned the book to the best-seller lists, after it was chosen for Oprah Winfrey's book club.
According to Israel Hayom, the book rose to prominence again when it was chosen as Oprah Winfrey's book of the month.
According to Israel Hayom, "Night" has so far sold more than ten million copies and has become one of the books most identified with the Holocaust.
Wiesel wrote dozens more books.

stations.title: In America: a commission, a medal, Bitburg

paragraphs.text: Wiesel came to the United States in 1956 and became a citizen there in 1963.
In 1978 President Jimmy Carter appointed him chairman of the President's Commission on the Holocaust.
Wiesel said that not all victims of the Holocaust were Jews, but all Jews were victims.
On April 19, 1985, President Reagan presented him with the Congressional Gold Medal.
At the ceremony Wiesel asked Reagan not to visit the cemetery in Bitburg, and told him that his place was with the victims.
Reagan visited the cemetery despite international protests.
At the opening of the Holocaust Museum in Washington, Wiesel said that his words were engraved in stone at the entrance to the building.
He said that as a Jew he was calling for something to be done to stop the bloodshed in the former Yugoslavia.
In a 1999 speech at the White House he said that in Kosovo the world was not silent this time, but responded.
According to the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, President Reagan presented Elie Wiesel with the Congressional Gold Medal on April 19, 1985.
On October 14, 1986, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Egil Aarvik, announced that Wiesel would receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Wiesel was chosen as a messenger to mankind, and his message is one of peace, atonement and dignity.
His candidacy was supported by previous Nobel laureates, among them Willy Brandt.
According to EBSCO, public reaction to the prize was favorable, with an attitude more serious than celebratory.
The prize was presented in Oslo on December 10, 1986.
In his acceptance speech Wiesel said that the honor belonged to all the survivors and their children, and to the Jewish people, with whose destiny he had always identified.
He asked whether he had the right to represent the multitudes who had perished, and answered that he did not.
He said that he had sworn not to be silent when human beings endure suffering and humiliation, and that neutrality helps the oppressor and not the victim.
He said that he had tried to keep memory alive and to fight those who would forget.
He said that action is the only remedy to indifference, the most insidious danger of all.
According to the Nobel Prize website, Wiesel saw the struggle against indifference as a struggle for peace.
He said that apartheid was, in his view, as abhorrent as anti-Semitism.
He said that he was sensitive to the plight of the Palestinians but deplored their methods, and that violence and terrorism are not the answer.
In his Nobel lecture Wiesel said that if anything can save humanity, it is memory.
He asked whether they had failed, and answered that he often thinks so.
He said that because he remembers he despairs, and because he remembers it is his duty to reject despair.
He said that perhaps we are powerless to prevent injustice, but we must never stop protesting.
He said that Israel, after two thousand years of exile and 38 years of sovereignty, still does not have peace.
In Oslo Wiesel spent hours on the telephone encouraging Jews who had been refused permission to emigrate from the Soviet Union.
According to EBSCO, Wiesel used the Nobel Prize to establish the Elie Wiesel Foundation for Humanity.
According to the Times of Israel, the foundation dealt with hatred and ethnic conflicts around the world.
Wiesel also received the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom and the rank of Grand-Croix of the French Legion of Honor.
In an interview, Wiesel said that the great disappointment of his life was that nothing had changed, and noted that too much indifference remained in the world.
Wiesel died on July 2, 2016, in New York.
Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said that the State of Israel and the Jewish people bitterly mourn his death.
According to the foundation's own website, Elie and Marion Wiesel founded the foundation in 1987, shortly after Elie won the Nobel Peace Prize.
According to Israel Hayom, Leon Wieseltier wrote in 1974 that Wiesel keeps the wound of Auschwitz open, and pours salt on every attempt at recovery.
According to EBSCO, some dissenters faulted Wiesel for not speaking out boldly enough against Israel's policies toward the Palestinians.
Wiesel was a longtime supporter of Israel, but was at times criticized for his closeness to Prime Minister Netanyahu.
Haaretz commentator Rogel Alpher wrote to Wiesel: "Netanyahu is my prime minister. You are not an Israeli citizen. You do not live here."
Wiesel said that in the Madoff affair he lost $15.2 million of the foundation's funds, as well as personal investments.

disagreements.question: On what date did Wiesel's father die?

versions.says: According to the Nobel Prize website: on January 29, shortly after arriving at Buchenwald
According to Encyclopaedia Britannica: on January 28, at Buchenwald

disagreements.question: How many books did Wiesel write?

According to Israel Hayom: more than 50 books

claims.text: ויזל אמר בנאומו שנשבע לא לשתוק כשבני אדם סובלים ומושפלים, ושניטרליות מסייעת לעושק ולא לקורבן.
claims.quote: And that is why I swore never to be silent whenever and wherever human beings endure suffering and humiliation. We must always take sides. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim.

claims.text: בנאומו אמר ויזל שניסה לשמר את הזיכרון ולהילחם במי שרוצים לשכוח.
claims.quote: That I have tried to keep memory alive, that I have tried to fight those who would forget

claims.text: לפי אתר פרס נובל, ויזל ראה במאבק באדישות מאבק לשלום.
claims.quote: Elie Wiesel saw the struggle against indifference as a struggle for peace.

claims.text: בנאום הקבלה אמר ויזל שהאפרטהייד נתעב בעיניו כמו אנטישמיות.
claims.quote: Apartheid is, in my view, as abhorrent as anti-Semitism.

claims.text: בנאום הקבלה אמר ויזל שהוא רגיש למצוקת הפלסטינים אך מוקיע את שיטותיהם, ושאלימות וטרור אינם התשובה.
claims.quote: there are the Palestinians to whose plight I am sensitive but whose methods I deplore. Violence and terrorism are not the answer.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל אמר ויזל שאם משהו יכול להציל את האנושות, זה הזיכרון.
claims.quote: Memory saved the Besht, and if anything can, it is memory that will save humanity.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל שאל ויזל אם נכשלו, והשיב שהוא חושב כך לעתים קרובות.
claims.quote: Have we failed? I often think we have.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל אמר ויזל שמפני שהוא זוכר הוא מתייאש, ומפני שהוא זוכר חובתו לדחות את הייאוש.
claims.quote: Because I remember, I despair. Because I remember, I have the duty to reject despair.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל אמר ויזל שאולי אין בכוחנו למנוע עוול, אך לעולם אסור שנחדל למחות.
claims.quote: There may be times when we are powerless to prevent injustice, but there must never be a time when we fail to protest.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל אמר ויזל שלישראל, אחרי אלפיים שנות גלות ו-38 שנות ריבונות, עדיין אין שלום.
claims.quote: And then there is Israel, which after two thousand years of exile and thirty-eight years of sovereignty still does not have peace.

claims.text: בהיותו באוסלו בילה ויזל שעות בטלפון בעידוד יהודים מסורבי עלייה מברית המועצות.
claims.quote: he spent hours on the telephone encouraging Jews who had been denied permission to emigrate from the Soviet Union

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, ויזל השתמש בפרס נובל כדי להקים ב-1987 את קרן אלי ויזל לאנושות.
claims.quote: Wiesel used his Nobel Prize to establish in 1987 the Elie Wiesel Foundation for Humanity.

claims.text: לפי Times of Israel, קרן אלי ויזל לאנושות הוקמה ב-1988 ועסקה בשנאה ובסכסוכים אתניים בעולם.
claims.quote: The Elie Wiesel Foundation for Humanity, which he established in 1988, explored the problems of hatred and ethnic conflicts around the world.

claims.text: ויזל קיבל גם את מדליית החירות הנשיאותית האמריקנית ואת דרגת גראנד-קרואה של לגיון הכבוד הצרפתי.
claims.quote: He also received the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom and the rank of Grand-Croix in France

claims.text: ויזל אמר בראיון שהאכזבה הגדולה בחייו הייתה ש"שום דבר לא השתנה", וציין שנותרה בעולם אדישות רבה מדי.
claims.quote: Too much indifference in the world, to the Other, his pain, and anguish, and hope.

claims.text: ראש ממשלת ישראל נתניהו אמר שמדינת ישראל והעם היהודי מתאבלים מרות על מות ויזל.
claims.quote: The State of Israel and the Jewish People bitterly mourn the passing of Elie Wiesel

claims.text: לפי ישראל היום, ליאון ויזלטיר כתב ב-1974 שוויזל שומר את הפצע אושוויץ פתוח בזריית מלח על כל ניסיון שיקום.
claims.quote: הפרויקט האישי שלו הוא לשמור את הפצע ששמו אושוויץ פתוח, על ידי זריית מלח עקבית על כל ניסיון שיקום

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, מתנגדים מסוימים האשימו את ויזל שלא דיבר בנחרצות מספיק נגד מדיניות ישראל כלפי הפלסטינים.
claims.quote: Some dissenters found fault with Wiesel for not speaking out more boldly against Israel’s policies toward the Palestinians.

claims.text: ויזל היה תומך ותיק בישראל, אך ננזף לעתים על קרבתו לראש הממשלה נתניהו.
claims.quote: Wiesel was a longtime supporter of Israel although he was criticized at times for his closeness to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanhayu.

claims.text: פרשן הארץ רוג'ר אלפר כתב לוויזל שנתניהו הוא ראש הממשלה שלו, ושוויזל אינו אזרח ישראלי ואינו חי בה.
claims.quote: Netanyahu is my prime minister. You are not an Israeli citizen. You do not live here.

claims.text: ויזל אמר שהפסיד 15.2 מיליון דולר מכספי הקרן בפרשת מיידוף, וכן השקעות אישיות.
claims.quote: Wiesel said he ended up losing $15.2 million in foundation funds, plus his and his wife

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, שנתיים אחר כך קיצר ויזל את הספר לכ-100 עמודים, תרגם לצרפתית ופרסם כ-La Nuit ב-1958.
claims.quote: Two years later, he radically shortened the volume to about one hundred pages, translated it into French, and published it as La Nuit (1958).

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיית השואה של מוזיאון השואה בוושינגטון, ויזל ואביו הועברו מאושוויץ לבוכנוואלד, ושם מת האב.
claims.quote: He and his father were later transported from Auschwitz to Buchenwald, where his father died.

claims.text: לפי אתר הקרן עצמה, אלי ומריון ויזל הקימו את הקרן ב-1987, זמן קצר אחרי שאלי זכה בפרס נובל לשלום.
claims.quote: Elie and Marion Wiesel founded The Elie Wiesel Foundation in 1987, shortly after Elie won the Nobel Peace Prize.

claims.text: לפי ספריית רייגן הנשיאותית, הנשיא רייגן הגיש לאלי ויזל את מדליית הזהב של הקונגרס ב-19 באפריל 1985.
claims.quote: [At this point the President presented Elie Wiesel with the Congressional Gold Medal.]

claims.text: ויזל, בן שש עשרה, היה עדיין בחיים כשחיילי בעלות הברית שחררו את המחנה ב-11 באפריל.
claims.quote: born September 30, 1928, Sighet, Romania

claims.quote: From Rogel Alpher in Haaretz:
claims.checker_note: audit: quote found on the fetched page

claims.text: הונגריה הייתה בת בריתה של גרמניה הנאצית. כבר ביולי–אוגוסט 1941 גורשו מהונגריה מאות מיהודי סיגט, ורבים מהם נרצחו בקמניץ-פודולסק, אבל רוב יהודי העיר נפגעו רק אחרי הפלישה הגרמנית במארס 1944.
claims.quote: In July–August 1941, hundreds of Jews from Sighet were deported from Hungary.
